candidateRows: The coherent affirmation of transcendental facts is best explained by the existence of God.
This supplies the principal inference from the existence and use of transcendental facts to God, directly addressing the debate motion.
After rejecting exclusively empirical constraints, Tyler introduces deductive and modest abductive formulations and defines transcendental facts as preconditions of rationality.
The necessary attributes of logical laws ultimately require a transcendent personal mind rather than naturalism or abstract Platonism.
This is the main explanatory bridge in Tyler's case, moving from the properties of logic through rejected alternatives to a personal divine ground.
Tyler attributes objectivity, necessity, timelessness, immateriality, and transcendence to logic, rejects conventionalism and Platonism, and argues that divine agency explains logical order.
Treating transcendental facts as brute or unknown does not defeat the divine explanation because God is instead a self-existing necessary fact.
The move defends the central divine-grounding inference against the alternative that logic needs no explanation or may remain unexplained.
The atheistic position that transcendental facts may be brute facts or have an unknown ground.
Tyler distinguishes divine necessity from brute existence, argues that naturalism cannot make transcendental facts self-explanatory, and rejects mere agnosticism as a defeater.
Positing one God as the common explanation of transcendental facts satisfies parsimony and broader explanatory virtues better than atheistic alternatives.
This move answers a major objection to the proposed divine explanation and offers the concluding comparative case for its scope, unity, and plausibility.
The skeptical use of parsimony to reject God as an unnecessary addition to explanations of transcendental facts.
Tyler argues that one divine ground does not multiply entities, contrasts it with brute facts or numerous separate explanations, and invokes explanatory scope and coherence.
Good evidence must be assessed by bias-reducing epistemic standards and should reliably support a sufficiently specific, testable hypothesis.
This establishes the con side's governing criterion for the motion: evidence for God must reliably discriminate that explanation rather than merely accompany belief.
Tyler's rejection of ordinary empirical constraints and his presentation of an abductive divine explanation.

Matt distinguishes evidence from good evidence, argues that subjective conviction is inadequate, stresses known cognitive and testimonial errors, and proposes repeatability, verification, specificity, falsifiability, and causal relevance.
Abductive selection of a likely explanation is unreliable when the candidate set is incomplete, especially for extraordinary hypotheses.
The move challenges the inferential method underlying Tyler's case by showing that consistency with observations does not establish a hypothesis's comparative likelihood.
Tyler's claim that God can be selected as the abductively best explanation of transcendental facts.
Using ordinary animals and extraordinary creatures as an analogy, Matt argues that compatibility with observed traces does not confirm additional extraordinary attributes.
A vague divine concept cannot function as a discrete hypothesis, so unexplained order or logic does not warrant an inference to God.
The objection directly attacks whether Tyler's proposed God is defined precisely enough for transcendental facts to count as discriminating evidence for it.
Tyler's proposed personal divine ground as the explanation for logic, rationality, and other transcendental facts.
Matt argues that classical-theist descriptions often remain generalized and that moving from a demand for explanation to an unspecified divine foundation is an unsupported leap.
Abductive arguments for supernatural causes lack the comparative data, exhaustive alternatives, and confirmed divine activity needed to establish likelihood.
This challenges the central probabilistic warrant of Tyler's inference by denying that anyone can calculate or compare the likelihood of divine causation.
Tyler's claim that God has high abductive warrant as the best available explanation for transcendental reality.

Matt requires a near-exhaustive candidate set and comparative frequency data, observes that no divine causal acts are confirmed, and rejects appeals from absent natural explanations to supernatural ones.
The obscurity, disagreement, and unfalsifiability surrounding God claims are contrary to what should be expected if a capable God supplied good evidence.
The move supplies an independent evidential challenge: a powerful God could make its existence clear, whereas actual disagreement and hiddenness fit that expectation poorly.
The affirmative claim that strong evidence for a classical-theist God already exists and supports reasonable belief.

Matt characterizes apologetic hypotheses as malleable, contrasts divine hiddenness with expected clear evidence, and notes persistent disagreement among believers about evidence and divine attributes.
Tyler's nonstandard evidentiary framework does not demonstrate God and may leave logic no more reliably grounded than competing accounts.
This is Matt's direct concluding answer to Tyler's case, disputing both its evidentiary method and the alleged reliability gained by grounding logic in divine choice.
Tyler's rejection of empirical epistemology and his abductive claim that an unchanging God grounds logical laws.

Matt argues that changing evidentiary categories requires an independent validation mechanism, questions whether divinely created laws could change, and concludes that the abductive case does not qualify as good evidence.
Shared use of logic establishes common ground but leaves the central question of its truth and possible foundation unanswered.
This frames Tyler's principal reply by distinguishing practical reliance on logic from the deeper explanatory question his transcendental case is intended to answer.
Matt's opening contention that Tyler had not supplied recognizable good evidence for God.
At the start of open discussion, Tyler accepts much of the shared account of reasoning but redirects attention toward whether logical truths have a foundation and are objectively true.
The basic laws of logic need no demonstrated transcendent realm or foundation and appear true independently of whether any God exists.
This supplies Matt's central alternative to transcendental theism: logical truths may simply hold necessarily without being entities grounded in a personal deity.
Tyler's claim that agreement about reasoning still requires an account of its truth and possible foundation.
Matt agrees on the basic logical principles but rejects the additional inference to a timeless realm, argues that they remain true without God, and raises the mutability dilemma.
Naturalism cannot ground transcendental facts, whereas the intelligibility of abstract truths as mental concepts supports their grounding in mind.
The move states the core positive transcendental inference from the alleged failure of naturalistic grounding to a mind-based explanation of logical abstractions.
Matt's argument that immutable laws would bind and therefore transcend God rather than be grounded in God.

Tyler distinguishes creating a universe that conforms to logic from creating logic itself, then argues that abstract truths are coherently understood as concepts in minds rather than freestanding entities.
Logical laws are descriptions of reality, and no case has been made that their truth requires any further grounding or explanation.
This directly opposes the principal theistic premise that logical necessity demands an ontological foundation beyond the fact that logical relations hold.
Tyler's claim that freestanding logical abstractions are incoherent and are intelligible by analogy with concepts in minds.
Matt treats logic and mathematics as descriptions derived from foundational logical identities and argues that asking why those identities are true may not be a cogent demand.
The universality of logic survives imagined and quantum cases, yet this gives no reason to add God as a necessary or inviolable foundation.
The move defends logical necessity against Tyler's contingency objection while maintaining that universality alone does not establish the proposed divine explanation.
Tyler's contention that treating logical truths through conditional thought experiments makes them contingent and arbitrary.
Matt explains that indeterminate phenomena still satisfy identity and noncontradiction, allows that a counterexample could undermine logic, and denies that usefulness or reliability establishes God.
Suspending judgment about a foundation is more parsimonious than positing an unevidenced timeless and spaceless being to explain logical laws.
This deploys burden of proof and parsimony against the central theistic inference, arguing that an unexplained God adds an entity without first establishing explanatory need.
Tyler's criticism that Matt's descriptivist account is unstable, vague, and avoids answering the proposed grounding argument.
Matt denies offering any rival foundation, says no need for one has been demonstrated, and rejects moving from uncertainty to a deity sharing the asserted transcendental attributes.
Reliable belief may use reasoning and abstraction, but claims about reality require empirical support somewhere in their justificatory chain.
The move clarifies the evidentiary standard driving the con case and explains why agreement on logic does not license Tyler's additional metaphysical conclusion.
Tyler's repeated characterization of Matt's evidentiary demands as a form of logical positivism.
Matt distinguishes his view from crude scientism, accepts evidence-backed reasoning and mathematics, and treats practical success as support for logic without claiming an ultimate foundation.
A valid argument is insufficient evidence for God unless its premises are shown true, because the debate requires soundness rather than validity alone.
This identifies the decisive alleged gap in the pro case: formal argumentative structure does not establish the truth of the premises or provide good evidence for God.
Tyler's assertion that he had already supplied a good explanatory argument that Matt had merely dismissed.
Matt accepts that an argument was presented but insists that its soundness remains undemonstrated and asks what evidence establishes the truth of its premises.
Abductive defense of philosophical premises can produce a sound argument, while demanding direct empirical support as the only evidence is self-defeating.
This is Tyler's principal methodological defense of the evidence offered for the transcendental argument and his counterattack on the con evidentiary standard.
Matt's objection that Tyler had shown validity but had not supplied evidence establishing the premises and soundness.
Tyler says philosophical discourse legitimately uses implication and abduction, denies that scientific repeatability is the sole route to reasonable belief, and alleges self-reference failure.
An epistemology that always ranks natural alternatives above God risks becoming unfalsifiable because any apparent evidence can be dismissed through another possibility.
The move challenges whether Matt's evidentiary framework could ever recognize evidence for God, making the admissibility and falsifiability of the con standard itself a central issue.
Matt's stated demand for empirical grounding and his practice of withholding assent where alternative explanations remain available.
Tyler asks what could falsify Matt's epistemology or count as good evidence for God if aliens, cognitive error, anecdote, quantum effects, or unexplained nature always remain preferable.
A capable God should know how to provide unmistakable, verifiable evidence of its existence, so the absence of such evidence is not a defect in scientific epistemology.
The move directly supplies the con side's governing answer about what divine evidence should accomplish and relocates the evidential burden from the skeptic to the proposed God.
Vela's claim that Dillahunty's epistemology cannot identify any evidence that would falsify it or establish God.

After Vela asks what could overcome naturalistic alternatives, Dillahunty says he cannot prescribe the exact evidence but an omniscient God could provide personally compelling and scientifically verifiable confirmation.
Dillahunty's claim that humanity is permanently unable to identify God merely assumes a restrictive scientific epistemology whose own falsification conditions remain unspecified.
This is the pro side's principal methodological objection: a standard used to reject theistic evidence must itself state what could count against it.
Dillahunty's contention that humans cannot distinguish God from delusion or advanced natural agents and therefore require divine verification.

Vela denies that inquiry is permanently stuck, rejects logical positivism, and argues that a scientific-style epistemology is inadequate if it demands falsifiability while offering no account of its own falsifier.
The limits of human inquiry do not discredit science; if a God made supernatural truth inaccessible to humanity's most reliable investigative method, responsibility lies with that God.
The move defends the con side's foundational evidentiary standard and turns the alleged inability to detect God into evidence against the proposed divine arrangement.
Vela's argument that an epistemology modeled on science is defective when it cannot specify what would falsify its stance toward God.

Dillahunty distinguishes practical inquiry from ultimate foundations, describes science as the most consistently reliable method available, and argues that no mechanism for investigating supernatural action has been demonstrated.
Theism offers an abductive foundation for reason, while Dillahunty's scientific evidentiary standard remains vulnerable because he has not supplied a clear falsification condition for it.
The move reconnects the exchange to the transcendental case for God and operationalizes the pro side's challenge with an extreme empirical example.
Dillahunty's claim that scientific inquiry is reliable and that the absence of an investigable supernatural mechanism counts against the divine arrangement.

Vela says God is the best foundation for reasoning, presses Dillahunty to state how his epistemology could be falsified, and asks whether an astronomically improbable divine message in the stars would count as evidence.

An extraordinary celestial message would count as evidence for God but would not by itself confirm Yahweh, especially when an omnipotent God could communicate directly and eliminate rival explanations.
This move gives a direct, discriminating answer to the central question by accepting evidence in degree while denying that an isolated anomaly establishes the proposed personal God.
Vela's challenge that a spectacular, astronomically improbable message written in the stars should satisfy Dillahunty's demand for evidence of God.

Dillahunty accepts the hypothetical as evidence toward God, denies that it alone warrants belief in Yahweh, cites unresolved alternatives, and argues direct divine communication would better fit the stated deity.
Rejecting even a maximally dramatic celestial sign as insufficient for belief shows that Dillahunty's professed openness is undermined by an evidentiary threshold that no proposed sign can reach.
The move crystallizes the pro side's charge that the skeptical standard is practically insulated from counterevidence even when confronted with an extreme confirming event.
Dillahunty's distinction between a celestial sign being evidence toward God and its being sufficient to warrant belief in Yahweh.
Vela explains that the hypothetical was intentionally extreme and argues that calling such an event evidential yet still belief-insufficient makes Dillahunty's openness to divine evidence doubtful.
Dillahunty's demand for an incontrovertible link to God is structurally unattainable because his framework always permits a naturalistic, brute-fact, or skeptical alternative.
This is a focused internal critique of the con standard, alleging that its permissible defeaters make any evidential route from an observed fact to God impossible.
Dillahunty's claim that the stellar sign is good evidence but needs a demonstrated pathway making God the uniquely best explanation.

Vela argues that rival natural explanations and appeals to unknown brute facts always remain available, then characterizes Dillahunty as requiring repeatable, independent linkage before belief could be rational.
Repeatable scientific confirmation is an ideal rather than a necessary threshold, since direct divine revelation could warrant the recipient's belief while remaining mere hearsay to everyone else.
The move blocks the charge that skepticism rules out all divine evidence by identifying a possible source of warrant while explaining why private revelation cannot publicly establish God.
Vela's assertion that Dillahunty requires scientifically repeatable and independently linked evidence before belief in God could ever be rational.

Dillahunty says his scientific standard describes the evidential ideal, concedes that an individual revelation might warrant belief, and argues that its private nature prevents it from supporting others.
The cumulative features of reality already provide sufficient evidence for God, and claims need evidence sufficient to their content rather than evidence labeled extraordinary.
This move affirms the pro side's positive evidential conclusion and states the epistemic rule by which Vela considers his transcendental and abductive considerations adequate.
Dillahunty's question why everyone lacks direct revelation if abstract arguments and features of reality do not provide adequate evidence.

Vela denies that universal private revelation is necessary, maintains that the previously discussed features of reality supply enough reason, and substitutes sufficient evidence for extraordinary evidence.
Private revelation may warrant its recipient without supporting anyone else, while increasingly extraordinary public claims rationally demand proportionally stronger evidence.
The move integrates the debate's two central evidentiary distinctions: first-person warrant versus transferable evidence, and ordinary claims versus claims requiring substantially stronger support.
Vela's repeated attempt to establish an internal-revelation standard and his rejection of the maxim that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

Dillahunty compares revelation to inaccessible personal experience, says outsiders cannot assess it, and uses escalating wallet claims to explain why evidence adequate for mundane claims may be inadequate for extraordinary ones.
The possibility that a person has private warrant does not make widespread religious belief reasonable or establish that billions possess such warrant.
This separates possible first-person justification from an argument capable of supporting the debated conclusion for other people.
Tyler's claim that billions may possess sufficient warrant for religious belief even if they cannot demonstrate it to Matt.
Tyler argues that private warrant can exist independently of public demonstration; Matt concedes its possibility while denying the population-level inference.
The allegedly subjective warrant is special to Tyler's theistic framework, while a God capable of revealing himself should provide a demonstration useful to others.
The move challenges both the claimed source of religious warrant and its inability to function as publicly useful support for God.
Tyler's contention that Matt's evidential standard pushes religious warrant wholly into an unfalsifiable subjective realm.
After Tyler calls the standard subjective and non-falsifiable, Matt argues that this problem arises from Tyler's special God-based warrant and hidden revelation.
The bare assertion that logic would remain applicable without God does not defeat the abductive arguments offered for God as necessary to transcendental facts.
This directly defends the motion-level claim that logical applicability depends on God and assigns a burden to proposed defeaters.
The audience assertion that the laws of logic would remain applicable to reality even if God did not exist.
An audience member denies that logic depends on God; Tyler answers that his prior abductive case supplies warrant unless a substantive defeater is given.
Non-natural transcendental principles can be supported through deductive, inductive, abductive, and mathematical reasoning, with God's mind supplying their coherent framework.
The answer states the proposed non-empirical methodology and connects non-natural truths to the divine grounding central to the motion.
The clarified challenge asking for a non-natural truth independently reachable by Tyler's methodology rather than by scientific investigation.
The repeated audience question presses Tyler for methodological examples; he cites identity over time and several forms of reasoning, then situates such truths in God's mind.
Counterfactual truths without a natural universe need not be independently existing entities, and claims of private religious warrant are no better validated than claims of ghost encounters.
It resists reifying transcendental truths and supplies an epistemic parity objection to treating religious conviction as adequate support.
Tyler's claim that transcendental truths would remain true without a natural universe and coherently exist within the mind of God.
Matt distinguishes reasoning within a thought experiment from an empty reality, broadens scientific method, and compares Christian warrant to unsupported supernatural testimony.
Defining God as the necessary ground of everything forecloses rival natural and divine models, even though the world can be examined without appealing to God.
This challenges the explanatory value of the necessary-ground thesis by arguing that it rules out alternatives through its setup rather than comparison.
Tyler's answer that asking whether logical principles would hold without God is meaningless because God is their necessary precondition.
Tyler treats a Godless counterfactual as incoherent; Matt grants why Tyler sees it that way but argues the framing makes every competing account impossible by definition.
The transcendental argument fails because its key grounding premise is insufficiently defended, while reason's practical reliability does not require a confirmable ultimate foundation.
The move reconstructs the central pro syllogism, identifies the disputed premise, and offers operational reliability as an alternative to divine grounding.
Tyler's central argument that confirmable transcendental facts require God because God is their necessary metaphysical ground.
Asked for Tyler's strongest point, Matt reconstructs the transcendental argument but says its defense improperly elevates facts to a meta-level and mistakes desired grounding for reliability.
Vague skepticism that merely proposes some unspecified alternative explanation is a personal disposition rather than a valid defeater of the presented arguments.
It identifies Tyler's principal objection to the con methodology: mere possibility of alternatives does not rebut an abductive explanatory case.
Matt's skeptical refusal to infer divine grounding from transcendental facts when their reliability can be assessed without a confirmed foundation.
Responding to the strongest-point prompt and Matt's critique, Tyler says skepticism may sound compelling but supplies no specific competing explanation or valid defeater.
Skepticism seeks methods that reliably track truth rather than cynically rejecting claims, whereas appeals to faith or unexplained brute status cannot justify conclusions.
This defends the con side's governing epistemic method against Tyler's charge that skepticism is merely an unsupported personal disposition.
Tyler's portrayal of skeptical alternatives as vague personal dispositions that do not constitute valid defeaters of his arguments.
Tyler dismisses vague skepticism as non-responsive; Matt defines skepticism as truth-oriented method selection and contrasts reliable investigation with faith and brute assertions.
Agreement that transcendental facts function does not answer the meta-level demand for their explanation and grounding, because such facts point beyond themselves.
This states the core explanatory step of the pro case: operational acceptance of transcendental facts leaves their metaphysical ground unaddressed.
Matt's objection that demonstrable facts and the functioning of transcendental principles suffice without Tyler's unclear tennis-ball analogy.
Matt says he does not understand the recurring analogy; Tyler explains that shared acceptance of transcendental facts leaves unanswered the separate question of what grounds them.
Vela's theistic position would be undermined by a plausible nonarbitrary account of transcendental facts that does not depend on God.
The move specifies an attempted falsification condition for the central claim that God uniquely explains transcendental facts.
Matt's earlier demand that Vela identify what could falsify his theistic explanation of transcendental facts.
In response to a question about changing his mind, Vela says a sufficiently plausible, nonarbitrary alternative explanation of transcendental facts would substantially weaken his view.
Vela's proposed falsification condition is circular because it presupposes that grounding is necessary and shifts the burden to proving a superior alternative.
It challenges both the burden of proof and testability of the debate's central claim that transcendental facts require divine grounding.
Vela's claim that his position is falsifiable if Matt supplies a more plausible grounding for transcendental facts.
Matt argues that Vela has not established the possibility or necessity of grounding and that demanding a rival grounding merely restates what would need to be disproved.
God is not hidden because creation, morality, transcendental facts, revelation, Jesus, and the resurrection collectively provide abundant evidence of God.
The answer directly asserts that transcendental facts form part of a cumulative evidential case for God, closely tracking the motion.
The audience challenge that an all-powerful and all-knowing God has not revealed himself in an obvious, convincing way.
Vela rejects the hidden-God premise and distinguishes the existence of extensive public evidence from whether a particular person finds that evidence psychologically compelling.
Vela's account is inconsistent if he says he does not know why God fails to reveal himself universally while also claiming God has revealed himself to everyone.
The alleged inconsistency pressures Vela's cumulative-evidence response to divine hiddenness and the claimed universality of revelation.
Vela's distinction between universal dramatic revelation and the claim that God is already generally revealed.
After clarifying two forms of the hiddenness question, Matt isolates a tension between Vela's professed uncertainty about universal disclosure and his universal-revelation claim.
If God wants everyone to know he exists and has an effective means of ensuring that knowledge but does not use it, that attributed desire is doubtful.
This is the developed logical form of the divine-hiddenness objection, testing the coherence of God's aims against observed nonbelief.
Vela's statement that God wants everyone to know he exists despite not giving everyone unmistakable direct revelation.
Matt converts the preceding discussion into a conditional objection: an unfulfilled divine aim combined with an available decisive mechanism counts against attributing that aim to God.
God's universal revelation creates an obligation to know him but does not imply that God intends to compel every person to form a settled belief.
The distinction is Vela's principal answer to the hiddenness objection and clarifies the scope of his claim about universally available evidence.
Matt's inference that unused universal direct revelation undermines Vela's claim about what God wants everyone to know.
Vela narrows his position from a divine intention to produce belief in everyone to a claim that creation reveals God sufficiently to place everyone under an epistemic obligation.
The universe's enormous size and uninhabitable planets are compatible with design because they may be necessary artifacts of a universe capable of permitting life anywhere.
The move rebuts an evidential objection to creation by arguing that apparently wasteful cosmic features follow from life-permitting conditions.
The audience contention that billions of lifeless planets are better evidence that humanity arose accidentally than that God created the universe.
Vela argues that a life-permitting cosmos may require its observed scale, expansion, and related byproducts, so lifeless planets do not independently establish accidental human origins.
Vela's account makes divine creation indistinguishable from a naturally occurring universe and appears to impose unnecessary constraints on an all-powerful God.
The critique attacks the explanatory value of theism by arguing that the observed cosmos looks natural and is not predicted by unlimited agency.
Vela's explanation that cosmic scale and uninhabitable planets are artifacts required by the features of a life-permitting universe.
Matt responds that an omnipotent creator could have made life without the vast naturalistic-looking apparatus, so Vela's explanation seems to constrain God after the fact.
A creator hypothesis is weakened when the chosen universe looks as though no creator intervened, especially if a creator could have made its role obvious.
The move directly contrasts the evidential expectations of divine creation with the apparently natural character of the observed universe.
Vela's clarification that the observed artifacts characterize this particular cosmos rather than limiting what God could create.
Matt shifts from whether God could create differently to why God selected a cosmos whose observable structure does not make divine involvement evident to skeptics.
The universe does look created because its transcendental features support that inference, so the dispute concerns how the shared observations are best explained.
This closing reply reconnects the cosmological exchange to the motion's central claim that transcendental features are evidence of creation.
Matt's challenge that the universe looks naturally occurring and unlike a world in which a creator made divine involvement obvious.
Vela answers that his earlier arguments make the observed transcendental features expected on creation and treats the remaining disagreement as competing inferences from common data.
